p: Saturday, November 7, ten thirty, the fields by the rec center. The AED was in a white box on the pavilion post, and Jordan found it before she found Ellie. Eighty yards to the near sideline. She walked it once, counting, because she was never going to stop doing that. Then the other way, out to the gate by the parking lot, where the ambulance would have come in. She didn't know which field he'd been on. She hadn't asked. Not today either.

Claire was in a folding chair at midfield with a thermos and didn't look up. You found the box. Jordan said she had. Claire unscrewed the thermos lid, filled it, and held it out, and Jordan took it and stood there with the other parents in the cold.

Ellie was playing defense, number 4, braids stuffed down the back of her shirt. A kid in orange came up the line with the ball and Ellie went at them like they owed her money. The kid gave it up. Ellie booted it out of bounds, hard, on purpose, and looked over at the sideline to see who'd seen.
Danny had been right. She was terrifying.

Tuesday, November 10, 9:20 in the morning, and the endorsement took Abby forty seconds to write. One dual to the practice area and back, steep turns, two stalls, a simulated engine failure over a sugar beet field east of Bennett that Jordan picked early and flew to like she'd been told where it was. On the ramp Abby uncapped the green pen and wrote it standing up, using the wing as a desk.
Practice area. Alone. Still under the shelf, still back by noon, still your card. She capped the pen. Now the part where you leave.
Cross-country. You go somewhere, you land, you come home. Thursday at four. Bring the chart, the plotter, and a pencil you don't love.

She'd bought the plotter the Saturday before, at the pilot shop by the FBO. Clear plastic, nine dollars, a ruler on one edge and a half moon of degrees in the middle. The man behind the counter had tried to sell her a forty dollar one with a light in it. She'd said her instructor said not the fancy one, and he'd nodded like he'd heard that before, which he probably had.

The other tool came out of Biscuit's door pocket. She'd found it in April, under the fuel tester and a parking receipt from 2019, and put it back without knowing what it was. Now she knew. An E6B flight computer, the aluminum kind, a slide rule on one side and a clear window over a sliding grid on the other, with D. REYES scratched on the back in capitals somebody had made with a key. On the wind side, in the middle of the frosted window, there was a pencil dot. A little circle around it. His last wind, whatever it had been.
She didn't erase it. She worked her first practice problem in the margin, around it.
That night Walt texted. Walt didn't text.
A text from Walt Herrera. Seven and a half months. Cross-country is where students stall. Weather, scheduling, nerves. I'd like to be wrong about this one.
She read it twice and decided it was the nicest thing he'd ever said to her, which told her something about Walt, and maybe about her.

Thursday, November 12, four in the afternoon, the briefing room. Jordan had come off a shift at seven that morning and slept until two, and she still had the station's coffee taste in her mouth. Abby had the Denver sectional unfolded across both tables with a coffee mug on each corner, the way you'd pin down a patient who didn't want an IV.

Jordan laid the new plotter from the little airport symbol at Centennial to the one east of Greeley and ran a pencil down the edge. Fifty three miles. It went north, a little east, and straight through the solid blue rings around Denver International. Not near them. Through the middle of the innermost one, where the number in the blue said the Bravo came all the way down to the ground.
Pretty line, Abby said. Your trip. Where does it go?

She erases the line and draws it again in pieces. East first, out over the Aurora Reservoir, then a turn northeast to Strasburg on I-70, then due north across open country to Roggen on I-76, then northwest into Greeley. Seventy two miles instead of fifty three. Next to each piece she writes the floor in a column, the way she'd write vitals: 80, 80, then 70 for a stretch, 80, 100, 80, nothing. Abby taps the 70 with her pencil. That's the one people miss. Everybody knows Centennial's 80. Nobody looks up out there. She checks the turn east of the reservoir. There's nothing on the ground at that corner, so make it a GPS point. Build it Sunday morning at the kitchen table, not on the climbout. Jordan writes BEND next to it. Abby considers this. Fine. It's a bend.
That evening she took the nav log to Claire's, because Claire had texted tamales, come eat them or I'll cry, and because Ellie had math homework and wanted company.

Ellie's homework was angles. Jordan's homework was angles. They sat across from each other at the kitchen table with the overhead light on, and after twenty minutes Ellie looked up from a protractor and asked where north was.
Jordan pointed out the window, at the Johnsons' garage. Ellie produced a little plastic compass from a cereal box and set it on the table. The needle settled a bit to the right of the garage.

Your north and my north are different. Mine's the map's. Yours is the magnet's. Around here they're about seven degrees apart. So who's right? Both of us. You just have to know how far apart. Ellie found that unsatisfying and said so.
Biscuit's compass card, taped under the compass. FOR N 30 60 E 120 150. STEER 001 031 062 092 121 150. FOR S 210 240 W 300 330. STEER 178 208 238 268 299 330. RADIOS ON. SWUNG 3/14/24, M. TRAN

The first row of her log: Centennial to BEND, true course 079 off the plotter. Wind at 9,000 forecast from 320 true at 16 knots. Her wind correction angle came out 8 degrees left, which made the true heading 071. Variation 7 east. Ellie watched her pencil hover.

MH 064. East is least, she says, in Abby's exact sing song, and Ellie fires back West is best before anybody asks her. So somebody taught her that. Jordan can guess who. Then the card. 064 is closest to 060, and 060 says steer 062, so two more. CH 066. Ellie leans across the tamales and reads the card upside down. So the airplane has its own north too? Sort of. Two degrees off. Ellie squints at it. Because it's old? Jordan, still writing: Because it's full of wires and an engine. Ellie decides this is Biscuit's fault and not Jordan's, which is pretty generous for a nine year old, and goes back to her protractor.

Monday, November 16. She'd flown the practice area alone that morning, 1.2 on the Hobbs, her first time out of sight of the tower by herself, and had spent most of it looking at the ground and saying the names of things out loud. Now it was the kitchen table and the altitude column.

Kneeboard, leg one, the floors. KAPA TO BEND: B 80. NOTHING ABOVE 7,700.. BEND TO STRASBURG: B 80.. STRASBURG TO ROGGEN: 80 FOR 3 MI. THEN 70 FOR ABOUT 7. THEN 80. THEN 100. THEN 80 AGAIN AT THE INTERSTATE.. ROGGEN TO KGXY: 80 FOR ABOUT 10. THEN NOTHING.. GROUND: ABOUT 5,000 TO 5,500 UNDER ALL OF IT. KGXY FIELD 4,697.

The Strasburg to Roggen leg was the long one, 26 miles due north across country with no towns to speak of, and its magnetic course was 351. Westbound. She knew the rule for westbound. She also knew the column.

She works it: 7,500 over ground at about 5,400 near Strasburg is 2,100 feet above it, under 3,000, so 91.159 doesn't apply, and she picks her numbers by the shelves. 6,700 is 300 under the 70. She draws a small step down in the altitude column at 3 miles and a step up at 10. Abby reads it that night and sends back one line. Good. Past Greeley, if you're ever above 3,000 AGL westbound, it's 8,500. Not today.

Thursday, November 19, the dual cross-country, Abby in the right seat with a thermos and a pack of yellow sticky notes. They flew the whole route the way Jordan had planned it: BEND, Strasburg, the step down under the 70, and for twenty minutes it was very calm and very flat.

Somewhere north of I-70 Abby said Hood, and Jordan put the foggles on, and for five minutes she flew whatever Abby said. Left turns. A climb. A long right turn. A descent. She lost count of the turns on purpose because Abby told her to.
I have the airplane. Hood off. When Jordan looked up, there was a sticky note over the GPS screen with a face drawn on it, a frown. GPS just died. You're lost. Your airplane.
Below: fields, brown and white, a dirt road, a center pivot like a long metal arm laid out in a circle. 6,600 on the altimeter. Nothing she recognized.

She rolls wings level on 360 and holds it, the PHAK's line running in her head. Ahead, maybe five miles, a straight gray line angles across her path toward the east-northeast with a thinner line beside it, an interstate and a railroad running together, which on this chart can only be I-76. She tunes the Denver VOR and listens: dash dot dot, dot, dash dot. Turns the OBS until the needle centers with a FROM flag. 028. She finds the 028 radial on the chart, follows it out from the station to where it crosses south of I-76. About twenty miles northeast of the Denver VOR, south of the interstate. Roggen's just ahead, where we'll meet the interstate. Abby peels off the sticky note. The GPS agrees within a mile. Abby writes something on her kneeboard and doesn't say what.

Twelve miles southeast of Greeley, Approach let them go. Radar service terminated, squawk VFR, frequency change approved. Jordan switched to Greeley's common frequency and listened, and nobody said anything for a long time, which at Centennial never happened.

The AWOS said wind calm, visibility 10, few clouds at 12,000, altimeter three zero two one. On her kneeboard she'd copied two lines from the Chart Supplement the night before: RWY 35 PREFERRED WHEN WIND LESS THAN 5 KTS. OIL DRILLING RIGS UP TO 120 FT ON AND INVOF ARPT. And the pattern altitude, 5,500 rounded, 800 feet above the field.
Greeley was spread across the windshield, the city on the left and the airport on its east side, two long runways in an L. Abby sat with her hands in her lap.

Greeley traffic, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, ten miles southeast, inbound for left traffic runway three five, Greeley. She crosses the field at 6,500, well above anything in the pattern, flies out to the west, descends to 5,500 away from the downwind, and turns back in on a 45. A Skyhawk comes up on the frequency, already on downwind. She sees it, calls it, follows it. Base, final, ten thousand feet of runway in front of her. Abby, as the mains touch: You could land three times on this one. Don't.

Saturday, November 21, 8 PM. She'd worked Friday into Saturday, a quiet one for once, and slept until two. Now the kitchen table again, with the finished log, a mug of tea gone cold, and the chart folded to the Denver panel so the route ran up the middle of the fold.

Nav log, N4791E, Sunday 11/22. TAS 105. Wind 320/16 (FB 9000). Var 7E. Dev from nearest card heading.. LEG 1. KAPA TO KGXY. CHECKPOINT TC WCA TH MH DEV CH DIST GS ETE FUEL ALT. BEND (RES.) 079 -8 071 064 +2 066 16.4 112 9 1.2 7500. STRASBURG 046 -9 037 030 +1 031 9.7 103 6 0.8 7500. ROGGEN 358 -5 353 346 +1 347 26.2 92 17 2.3 7500/6700/7500. KGXY 324 -1 323 316 0 316 20.1 89 14 1.8 7500. TOTAL 72.4 NM, 46 MIN. CRUISE 6.1 TAXI 1.0 CLIMB 1.0 8.1 GAL. LEG 2. KGXY TO KCFO. ROGGEN 144 +1 145 138 0 138 20.1 121 10 1.3 7500. STRASBURG 178 +5 183 176 -2 174 26.2 117 13 1.8 7500/6700/7500. KCFO 290 +4 294 287 -1 286 9.2 91 6 0.8 DESC 6500 (B 70). TOTAL 55.5 NM, 29 MIN. CRUISE 3.9 2.0 5.9 GAL. PLAN B: EAST AROUND ANYTHING THAT BUILDS. NEVER WEST (BRAVO). OR BACK TO KGXY.. LEG 3. KCFO TO KAPA. BEND 170 +4 174 167 -2 165 10.0 119 5 0.7 6500 (B 70). KAPA 260 +8 268 261 -2 259 16.4 96 10 1.4 7500. TOTAL 26.4 NM, 15 MIN. CRUISE 2.1 2.0 4.1 GAL. DAY: 154.3 NM FLOWN, 111.8 POINT TO POINT. FUEL 18.1 GAL. LAND WITH AN HOUR (8.0).

Flight plan, leg one, the way the app laid it out. AIRCRAFT: N4791E. C172.. PILOT: JORDAN E. REYES, AURORA CO.. DEPARTURE: KAPA, 1540Z.. ROUTE: BEND (USER WAYPOINT 39 37.2N 104 30.0W), STRASBURG, ROGGEN.. CRUISING ALTITUDE: 7,500 (6,700 NORTH OF STRASBURG UNDER CLASS B 7,000). TRUE AIRSPEED: 105 KTS.. DESTINATION: KGXY. ESTIMATED TIME EN ROUTE: 0 HR 53 MIN.. FUEL ON BOARD: 3 HR 00 MIN.. PERSONS ON BOARD: 1. AIRCRAFT COLOR: WHITE, MAROON STRIPE.. REMARKS: STUDENT PILOT. SOLO CROSS-COUNTRY.
The app had a button at the bottom that said FILE. She'd filled it in twice to be sure. Under it, smaller, another one: ADD STOP.

Three plans, three ETAs. She writes the closing times on her kneeboard in red, under each leg, with the half hour added: CLOSE BY 10:03. CLOSE BY 11:10. CLOSE BY 12:30. Then she texts Abby the times, because Abby says to tell somebody too and Abby is somebody. Abby: close every one. I'll know. Then: BEND is a good name.

Sunday, November 22, 6:40 in the morning, the briefing room, still dark outside. Abby had come in on a Sunday to review the planning, which 61.93 said she had to, and she'd brought two breakfast burritos from the place on Arapahoe Road, which nothing said she had to. She pushed one across the table without comment.

Weather, printed at 6:32 AM. METAR KAPA 221253Z 32006KT 10SM FEW120 M04/M12 A3016 RMK AO2. TAF KAPA 221120Z 2212/2312 32008KT P6SM FEW120. FM221800 34008KT P6SM SCT025. PROB30 2221/2224 4SM -SHSN BKN060. FM230100 34006KT P6SM SKC. FB DATA BASED ON 220600Z, VALID 221200Z, FOR USE 0900-1800Z. FT 3000 6000 9000 12000 18000. DEN 3216-06 3022-12 2934-24. GFA, PLAINS E AND NE OF DENVER: ISOLD -SHSN DEVELOPING AFT 17Z. BASES 8000-9000 MSL. VIS 1-3SM IN SHSN.

She did the times out loud. Twenty one hundred Zulu, minus seven: two in the afternoon. Seventeen Zulu: ten in the morning. The TAF only covered five miles around Centennial. The graphical forecast covered the space in between, which was where she'd actually be.

Her card was above the mag switch. On Monday, at the kitchen table, with Abby on speaker, she'd added a line at the bottom for cross-countries: CEILING 5,000 AGL, VIS 10, AND A WAY OUT ON EVERY LEG. Abby finished her burrito. Tell me the plan. Then tell me what turns you around.

She lays it out in order, the way she'd hand off a patient. Departure 8:40, Greeley by 9:35, fuel and close and file, out by 10:05, Space Port by 10:40, home by noon. One o'clock is the line. A shower on any leg: east around it, at least five miles, because west of the route is the Bravo. If east isn't open, back to Greeley and wait. Abby listens to all of it, nodding at nothing, and then uncaps the green pen and writes the second endorsement in her logbook, slowly, the way she never writes anything. Known conditions. That's the phrase in the reg. You just told me what they are.
The club chat from the night before was still open on her phone.
A message from Russ Kim. biscuit's back from the burger run. 27 by the stick, 13 and a half a side, so 24 usable. self serve card reader at APA is down again, sorry, not my fault, i blame the reader
A message from Marisol Tran. Truck can come Sunday, there's a callout fee. Greeley has fuel. Jordan, the selector's sticking short of BOTH again. Lift and twist, feel for the click, don't force it.

7:35 AM. Minus four on the ramp and the sky clean and pale over the plains. Walt was at the tie down, which on a Sunday morning surprised her until she remembered he'd been a dispatcher for thirty years and probably hadn't slept in on a weekend since the eighties. He had a coffee in each hand and gave her one. She dipped both tanks with the clear tube. Thirteen and a half a side, near enough. Twenty four usable.
Walt looked at her nav log over his glasses. Every release I ever signed had one number on it I cared about more than the others. What do you land with?

Leg one is 8.1. I land at Greeley with about 16, two hours. I top off there and land everywhere after that with two or more. Walt nods slowly. And if Greeley's pump is down too? She hadn't thought of that. Then I have 16 at Greeley, and the rest of the day needs 10 plus my hour. I'd wait or call the truck. I wouldn't leave. That's an alternate, he says. Most students think an alternate is a place. It's a decision you made before you needed it.
8:12 AM. A text from her mother.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Where today.
A text from Jordan Reyes. Greeley, then a stop near Watkins, then home. About three hours.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Text me when you're down. Each time.
In the flight bag, next to the green notebook, her logbook lay open to the new page.

Jordan's logbook, endorsements. 11/19/26. I certify that Jordan E. Reyes has received the required solo cross-country training. I find they have met the applicable requirements of 14 CFR 61.93 and are proficient to make solo cross-country flights in a Cessna 172N aircraft, airplane single-engine.. Limitations: Day VFR only. Ceiling 5,000 AGL or higher and visibility 10 SM or better at departure, destination, and en route reporting points. Remain at least 5 SM from any precipitation. Surface wind 10 knots or less, gusts no more than 5 over, crosswind component 5 knots or less. FLIGHT FOLLOWING ON EVERY LEG. No Class B. On the ground at KAPA by 1300 local.. /s/ 11/19/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027. 11/22/26. I have reviewed the cross-country planning of Jordan E. Reyes. I find the planning and preparation to be correct to make the solo flight from KAPA to KAPA via BEND, Strasburg, and Roggen with landings at KGXY and KCFO in a Cessna 172N aircraft on 11/22/26. Limitations of the 11/19/26 endorsement apply and are met.. /s/ 11/22/26 A. Strand 3418862CFI RE 06-30-2027
The capitals weren't for her, Abby had said, they were for the endorsement. Jordan had decided to believe that.

Runup on Alpha near the end of three five right, the left door latched top and bottom, both of them touched. Mags, carb heat, the selector lifted and twisted to BOTH until it clicked. Centennial Ground, Niner One Echo, ready for departure, runway three five right. Niner One Echo, monitor tower. Then tower, and the takeoff, wind three two zero at six, right turn eastbound approved, the door holding, the reservoir coming up blue and flat on the left of the nose, and then the tower: Niner One Echo, frequency change approved.

Denver Approach, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, four miles east of Centennial, climbing through seven thousand for seven thousand five hundred, request flight following to Greeley. A man's voice gives her a code. She reads it back and dials it in, and he says Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, radar contact, four miles east of Centennial, maintain VFR at or below seven thousand five hundred. Level at 7,500 she asks him for a minute off the frequency, opens the flight plan with Flight Service, and comes back, and BEND comes up on the GPS where she put it at the kitchen table, and the reservoir slides under the nose right on time.

8:57, Strasburg, right on time: the interstate, the grain elevator, the little grid of streets, and she turned north onto 347 and wrote the time on the log. Three miles later she stepped down to 6,700 for the 70.

9:04. By the log she should have been ten miles past Strasburg at 9:03 and a half. She checked her position against a section road crossing she'd marked, and then against the GPS, which agreed with the road: ten miles north of Strasburg, a mile left of the line. West. Toward Denver. Off to her left, fifteen miles or so, the white peaks of Denver International's tent roof sat on the horizon like laundry somebody forgot to bring in.
Heading indicator first, then the compass. Gyro, 347. The compass wobbled around for a bit and then settled on 343.

Gyro first: wings level, speed steady, the middle of the compass swing, 343. She resets it. So she'd been flying 343 the whole time, four degrees left of the plan, and that's most of the mile. The rest is wind. One mile off in ten is six degrees of track error: four from the gyro, two from the wind. So the heading that holds the line is 349. One mile back in sixteen is about four more. She turns to 353 on the newly honest gyro and watches the GPS needle start to walk back toward center. Ten miles in seven minutes is 86 knots, not 92: more headwind than the forecast. Sixteen miles at 86 is 11.3 minutes. ROGGEN 0915. At 9:15 the needle touches center and the interstate and the railroad come out from under the nose together, and she says Roggen to nobody.

Greeley went by the way it was supposed to. A left downwind for 35 behind nobody, a landing she was proud of, the fuel pit, the flight plan closed and the next one filed, a text to her mother: Down at Greeley. Her mother: Ok. She was off again at 10:05 with Approach giving her a new code, southeast at 7,500 toward Roggen, the low sun just right of the nose.

She saw it from fifteen miles out and didn't understand it at first. Ahead, a little right of the nose, a piece of the sky had gone gray. A flat dark base, maybe eight thousand feet, and under it a soft curtain reaching all the way to the fields, with lighter streamers hanging off its edges that didn't reach anything. It hadn't been there at Greeley. By Roggen, 10:17, it was right on her line to Strasburg, about twelve miles ahead, a few miles across, drifting southeast the way the winds aloft said it would. Slow.
To its right, west, the sky was clear all the way to the tent roof and the shelves. To its left, east, clear and bright over empty country all the way to I-70. Behind her Greeley sat in sunshine.

She doesn't turn at Roggen. She notes the time, 10:17, and keeps the heading she has, 138, which runs southeast down the clear side. Denver Approach, Niner One Echo, deviating east for a snow shower, then direct Strasburg. Niner One Echo, roger, no traffic observed in that direction. On the kneeboard: 19 miles to a point ten miles east of her line, out ahead of the shower because it's drifting toward her return leg, 121 knots, nine and a half minutes. Then a true course of 223 to Strasburg, 14.8 miles, which the crab and the variation bring back to 223 on the compass, 106 knots, eight and a half minutes. STRASBURG 1035. Four and a half minutes longer than the plan, and six tenths of a gallon. At 10:26 she turns. The shower slides by on her right, close enough to see the snow inside it moving, the streamers of virga glowing white where the sun gets under them, and then it's behind her and I-70 is ahead, and Strasburg is exactly where she left it.

Strasburg, then west down the interstate toward the Space Port with the ATIS in her ear: wind three three zero at eight, visibility one zero, few clouds at two thousand five hundred, landing runway three five. She was under the 80. She called the tower from eight miles east, then stepped down to 6,500 as she passed under the 70.
Cessna Niner One Echo, Space Port Tower, enter right downwind runway three five, report midfield.

On the downwind, with the long runway off her right wing, the tower came back. Niner One Echo, extend downwind, number two following a Citation on a four mile final. Caution wake turbulence. She found it, a small white jet low on final, gear down, catching the sun. She called it in sight. It looked harmless from there. Abby had told her what they all look like from there.

The tower calls her base. She turns final a little high on purpose and keeps the picture steep, above where the jet came down, and watches for its touchdown: a puff off the mains about a thousand feet down the runway. She aims for a spot well past it, which on 8,000 feet of runway costs her nothing at all. Her wheels touch beyond the puff. The Citation is already turning off ahead of her, small and white and harmless, and she lets out a breath she'd been keeping since the downwind.
She was on the ground at the Space Port at 10:43, which was three minutes later than the log, and she taxied to the FBO behind a lineman with orange wands who waved her in like she was a 737.

Mixture, mags, master. The propeller stopped. She sat with her hands in her lap the way she had after the discovery flight in April, and then she did the things in order. She called Flight Service and closed the plan. She texted her mother: Down at the Space Port. Her mother: What is a space port. Watkins. Text me from home.
Then she dipped the tanks out of habit and wrote the number on the log next to the time, in pencil, the way Walt wrote everything.

Inside, the FBO was warm and empty, a television on mute with the radar loop running and a vending machine that sold hot chocolate for a dollar fifty. She got one and sat in a leather chair by the window with Danny's headset on the seat next to her. On the screen, the little green blob that had been her shower drifted southeast past Byers and came apart. Home was clear. She had two hours before Abby's line and needed fifteen minutes of them. She stayed in the chair anyway.
Somewhere in the second half of the hot chocolate she noticed it.

Since 7:10 that morning, since Abby capped the green pen, she hadn't thought about him. Not at the runup. Not at BEND, or Strasburg, or the gyro that had drifted four degrees, or Greeley, where she'd stood on the ramp with his headset around her neck and the wind going through her coat. Not at the curtain. Three and a half hours. She'd had his headset on her head the entire time, and his E6B in the side pocket with his pencil dot on it, and she'd flown his airplane to Greeley, which was a place he'd flown, and she had not thought about Danny once.

It landed on her like forgetting a birthday. Like walking past the house of somebody whose funeral you went to and noticing you'd been humming. Eight months, and the first three free hours she'd had, she'd spent them without him and hadn't noticed until they were over. She put the cup down. She looked at the headset. She felt, for a minute, about as bad as she'd felt in March.
Then she put the headset on and went home.

The leg home was fifteen minutes and nothing happened in it. South from the Space Port under the 70, BEND coming up on the GPS where she'd built it, a right turn at BEND, the reservoir sliding by on the right, Centennial Tower giving her a right downwind for three five right and a landing she made without hurrying. She closed the third flight plan from the tie down at 11:58, chained Biscuit down tight, and texted her mother Home. Her mother sent back a heart, which she had never done before, and then, a minute later, as if to correct the record: Ok.
Claire texted while she was putting the cover on.
A text from Claire Reyes. El wants to know if Greeley smells. She says her dad told her it did.
A text from Jordan Reyes. Didn't notice. Had the vents closed. Tell her I'll ask.

She sat in the left seat with the door open and took out the green notebook. On Monday she'd found the page and folded the corner down without reading it, because she'd decided she'd read his first cross-country after she'd flown hers, and not before. It was July. Eleven years ago.

Danny's logbook, a page from July, eleven years ago. July 18. FIRST SOLO XC!!! C152 52B from the school. KAPA, Greeley, Front Range, KAPA. 2.6 on the Hobbs. Planned 2.2. You can see where this is going.. Went around the east side like a good boy. Strasburg, fine. Then I got to the next interstate and followed it, and it turns out you're supposed to cross that one, because it goes to Nebraska. Climbed. Read a water tower: WIGGINS. Wiggins is not Greeley. Turned to the heading I should have been on in the first place, found the river, found Greeley by the smell. Feedlots. You could land on that smell.. Front Range tower lady said "Welcome to Front Range" like she meant it. Bought a Coke. Called nobody.. Here's the thing I want on the record. For two and a half hours I did not think about one other thing. Not work, not money, not the guy at the shop, not anything. Just the next checkpoint and the gas and the next checkpoint. Nobody tells you that's the best part. It's not the view. It's the quiet in your head.. Jordan thinks too much. She'd like this. She'd never admit it.
She read the last line again. Then the one before it.

The guilt from the FBO came back for a second when she got to the end, and then it went, the way a pager tone hangs in your ear after the pager's quiet. Two and a half hours of quiet in your head, he'd called it. He wrote that in July with a Coke from the Front Range FBO sweating on the page, you could see the ring, and he put her name under it. She'd gotten three and a half. He'd have been smug about that on her behalf. He'd have said she beat his time and got lost less, and she'd have said Wiggins wasn't even in the same county, and he'd have done the bark.
She didn't feel bad anymore. She sat a while longer in the cold cockpit and didn't think about much.

Then she took Danny's E6B out of the side pocket and looked at the wind side. His pencil dot, with the little circle around it. She'd worked every problem for two weeks around it, and she'd thought more than once about rubbing it out with her thumb. She put it back in the pocket the way it was.

Walt came out of the hangar as she was leaving, with the club fuel log on a clipboard and the Greeley receipt stapled to it. He looked at the fuel column, then at her. That's a column I'd have signed. He tucked the clipboard under his arm. Eight months. Four left. I'm starting to think I'll be wrong. Then, because he was Walt: Starting.
That night, at 9:22, the phone buzzed on the kitchen table next to the folded chart.
